explanations.explanation: Famine is right, baker. The text says that when Elisha returned to Gilgal, "…there was a famine in the land." Food was running short, and that's the setting for everything that happens around this pot. A famine and a big pot of stew. I think everybody was watching that pot.

No war in this passage, friend. The text says "…there was a famine in the land." Nobody is fighting here, they're sitting at Elisha's feet. The trouble is an empty-ish pantry, not an enemy at the gate.

No plague here, baker. The verse says "…there was a famine in the land." That means food was running short, and the text names no sickness. The sons of the prophets are sitting at Elisha's feet when he tells his attendant to put on the large pot.

Not quite, baker. The text says the man cut the gourds into the stew "…though no one knew what they were." Nobody at that pot could name them, not even the man who picked them. Cutting up a mystery ingredient and tossing it in? I've done that with a jar from the back of the pantry, and it never ends well.

That's right, baker. The text says he cut them into the pot "…though no one knew what they were." Wild gourds from a wild vine, and not one person could name them. That's a lot of trust to put into a stew.

explanations.answer: There is death in the pot
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. They cried out, "There is death in the pot, O man of God!" Notice they called out to Elisha, the man of God, right away. They knew who to take the problem to, and that's a good habit for any of us. Then the text says they could not eat it.

explanations.answer: The stew is far too bitter
explanations.explanation: Close in spirit, but that's not what they said. The text says they cried out, "There is death in the pot, O man of God!" The words are much sharper than "too bitter." They tasted it and sounded the alarm right away.

Nope, nothing about a boil-over, baker. The men tasted the stew and cried out, "There is death in the pot, O man of God!" The trouble was inside the stew, not spilling out of the pot. The text says they could not eat it.

Not this time, baker. After they cried out, the text says plainly, "And they could not eat it." They stopped, and they took the problem to Elisha. Honestly, that's smarter than the time I ate a batch I KNEW was off, just to be polite.
You got it, baker. The text says, "And they could not eat it." Nobody pushed through it and nobody played hero. They had a problem and Elisha was right there to hear it.

Flour is it, baker. Elisha said, "Get some flour." and he threw it into the pot. Then he said, "Pour it out for the people to eat." The text says "…there was nothing harmful in the pot." He didn't dump the stew, he went for the flour.

Salt makes sense, friend, but that's not what the text says. Elisha said, "Get some flour." and he threw it into the pot. After that, "…there was nothing harmful in the pot." I'd have guessed salt too, I'm not above that.

Oil is a good guess, baker, but the text says something else. Elisha said, "Get some flour." and then he threw it into the pot. Then there was "…nothing harmful in the pot." Oil shows up in a different story around Elisha, a widow's jar of oil (2 Kings 4:2), but in this one it's flour.

Right, baker. The text says, "And there was nothing harmful in the pot." Elisha threw in the flour, told them to pour it out, and the stew was no longer a problem. The text doesn't explain how it happened, and I won't pretend to.
Not false, baker. After Elisha threw the flour in, the text says, "And there was nothing harmful in the pot." The problem was gone. He told them to pour it out for the people to eat.

Yes, baker. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat…" Twenty loaves were headed for the people, not set aside for someone important. The man from Baal-shalishah brought the loaves, and Elisha said to give them to the people.
Right, baker. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat…" The bread was for eating, plain and simple. In a famine, that's the best use for a sack of loaves.

No king in this one, friend. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat…" The loaves were for the people, not for a palace. The man from Baal-shalishah brought bread, and Elisha said to give it to the people.
Nobody's opening a bread stand here, baker. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat…" There's no selling in the verse, just giving. The bread was meant for eating.
Not the priests, friend. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat…" The text doesn't send the loaves to any priests. They were for the people to eat.

explanations.answer: There are a hundred men to feed
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The servant asked, "How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men?" He did the math and the math looked rough. I think I'd have asked the exact same question, probably with a worse face.

explanations.answer: The bread was meant for the priests
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. The servant asked, "How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men?" His problem was the numbers. Twenty loaves, a hundred men, and a lot of empty hands.

explanations.answer: The loaves are too hard to eat
explanations.explanation: Nothing about hard bread, baker. The servant asked, "How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men?" His question was about twenty loaves and a hundred men. The bread itself was barley bread from the first ripe grain.

explanations.answer: They will eat and have some left over
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Elisha said, "for this is what the LORD says: ‘They will eat and have some left over.’…" Elisha gave the servant that word before anyone had taken a single bite. A hundred men, twenty loaves, and the LORD says there's more than enough.

explanations.answer: Each man will get only a small piece
explanations.explanation: That's what the math says, baker, but not what the LORD says. Elisha told his servant, "…this is what the LORD says: ‘They will eat and have some left over.’…" Left over means there's more than enough, not a sliver apiece. The servant was counting loaves, and the LORD was talking about something bigger.

explanations.answer: The bread will last until the famine ends
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The word of the LORD was, "They will eat and have some left over." It says nothing about how long the bread would last or when the famine would end. The promise was about this meal, and it was a good one.
